newsitem.title: USA: Fast food eateries serve up collectibles with burgers.
newsitem.headline: Fast food eateries serve up collectibles with burgers.

text.p: Kids are not the only ones rushing in to their favourite burger joint to pick up the latest puppet, plastic car or movie character toy. Adults can be found cutting in line to get the same items to add to their own collections.
The nation is not only craving fast food but is caught up in a craze for fast food stuff.

"We live in a McDonald's museum," said John Larsen of Colusa, Calif., who along with his wife, Eleanor, have been collecting McDonald's memorabilia for nearly 20 years and estimate they live with more than 60,000 items.

"It's all on the walls and floor-to-ceiling everywhere," he laughingly admitted. "Toys are just a small part of the collection," he said, adding that just about anything related to fast food is collectible -- from buttons, cups and bags to caps, stickers and signs.
"I've ate thousands of those funny little hamburgers," he said.

Nowadays, people can go in a restaurant and buy most items, Larsen said, which can be a relief to anyone over age 12 who does not want to ask for a kid's meal and catch a smirk from the person bagging the order.
Among collectibles, the common toys can be had rather cheaply for a few dollars, while the more elaborate and often themed bags and boxes the stuff came in tends to be more valuable.

"When (McDonald's) started, the box was meant to be an advertising ploy, but then the toy picked up in interest and they saw the gold mine," Joyce Losonsky, co-author of the book "McDonald's Happy Meal Toys in the U.S.A.," said.
If you are lucky enough to own a limited promotional Mayor McCheese Happy Meal bag from 1975 -- minus ketchup stains -- Losonsky's book says it would be worth $75-$100 to a serious collector.
And if Mayor McCheese has proclaimed you a McDonald's citizen on an official certificate, that would go for about $15-$20.
Other early, decorated Happy Meal boxes from 1977 to 1980 have a value range of around $25 to $200 depending on condition, design and availability.
What exactly is the draw to this memorabilia?

"Collecting is McFun," Losonsky chuckled. "We all laugh all the time ... you can add 'Mc' to anything. The toys follow whatever the fad is. It's Americana because you see phases that America goes through," she said, using movie tie-ins such as "Star Wars", "E.T." and "101 Dalmations" as an example.

"I think it has a lot to do with people's emotional experience with McDonald's ... and growing up," Jane Hulbert, a McDonald's spokesperson at its Oak Brook, Ill., headquarters, said of the fascination with fast food collecting.
"Often it's a first place a child has an out-of-home meal, a teenage first date or someone's first job after mowing the grass," she said of the attachment.
The McDonald's Collectors Club boasts some 1,350 members in the United States and abroad, said Linda Gegorski, the club's secretary who co-founded it in 1990 in Fremont, Ohio.
"I rented the Holiday Inn and sent out registration forms hoping to get 10 replies," she said.

Although other fast food chains offer collectibles, McDonald's has taken off because of their promotional items "over and above the children's meals... The toy most people would probably die for is a box and set of two colouring books from 1988, from the 'Little Martin Luther King' promotion (marketed in) Detroit," Gegorich said. "It was a very limited Black History Month series."
The paper books were easily damaged and often thrown away, which would explain the top mint condition price of $1,000 each commanded at the club's charity auction, she said.
"The price guide has it at up to $200, however, at an auction, people get carried away and they want it," she said.

Harder to find premiums that were recalled -- like the 1993 miniature holiday Barbie in a snow globe that leaked, listed at $75-$100 in Losonsky's price guide, or the extremely limited 1986 Story of Texas book sets, priced at $65-$150 -- can send collectors into a trading frenzy.
Even Mr. Potato Head made it into Happy Meals in 1987. The first batch can fetch $20-$25. A second Potato Head series in 1992 is worth around $3.50.

Beyond the toys and packaging, even a particular display sign on a restaurant counter ($125) or hanging from the ceiling ($250), the polyester uniforms and badges and a store's translites -- the plastic picture on the drive-thru marquee or inside that lights up -- can be a hot commodity.
Translites spanning the years have had prices ranging from $250 for a Happy Meal display; $125 "We Buy Jokes" lighted board and $100 for Ronald McDonald holding a toothbrush on a 1986 sign.
"Each store has one of these," Losonsky said. "People will frame them and put them in their homes."
"It's a fun hobby. It can cost as little as $1 and go up to what you want it to. It's neat stuff," John Larsen said.
Losonsky added, "It's puttering around. They make enough for everybody. It's a real positive thing that spans all generations" of collectors.
